title: Power of Attorney Cost: Types, State Signing Rules and Fees (2026)
description: What a power of attorney costs, the types of POA, notary and witness rules in 9 large states, and what makes a lawyer-drafted POA cost more.
h1: How much does a power of attorney cost?
summary: The signing formalities for a power of attorney are inexpensive (a California notary may charge up to $15 per signature), so the cost is mostly legal time. At Clio's national average of $349 an hour, 1.5 hours of lawyer work is about $524. Execution rules vary: Florida and New York require a notary and two witnesses, Texas requires notarization for a durable POA, and California and Michigan accept a notary or two witnesses.
body:
Types of power of attorney

A power of attorney (POA) lets you, the principal, name an agent to act for you. The type you need affects how much drafting and advice it takes.

  • General (financial) POA: broad authority over money, property, banking and taxes.
  • Limited or special POA: one task or period, such as selling a car or closing on a house while you are away.
  • Durable POA: stays in effect if you lose capacity. This is the version most people want for planning, and some states require specific wording or formalities for it, as Texas and Michigan do [2][8].
  • Springing POA: takes effect only on a stated event, usually incapacity. It can be harder to use because someone must prove the event happened.
  • Health care POA: names someone to make medical decisions. It is often bundled with a living will or advance directive and follows separate state rules.

Signing rules: notary and witnesses by state

A POA that is not executed correctly may be refused by a bank or a court. The rules differ more than most people expect: some states require a notary, some require witnesses, and some require both.

Financial power of attorney signing requirements in 9 large states (checked October 11, 2026)
StateExecution requirements
CaliforniaDated and signed; then either notarized or signed by two qualifying witnesses [1]
TexasDurable POA must be signed and acknowledged before a notary or other officer who can take acknowledgments [2]
FloridaSigned by the principal and two subscribing witnesses, and acknowledged before a notary [3]
New YorkStatutory short form: signed, initialed and dated, acknowledged before a notary, and witnessed by two people who are not agents or gift recipients; the notary may be one witness. Agents must also sign and acknowledge [4]
PennsylvaniaDated and signed; acknowledged before a notary; two adult witnesses if signed by mark or by someone else for the principal; the agent cannot be the notary or a witness [5]
GeorgiaSigned, attested by one competent witness who is not an agent, plus a second attestation under the deed-attestation statute (O.C.G.A. §44-2-15) [6]
North CarolinaSigned and acknowledged; a signature acknowledged before a notary is presumed genuine [7]
MichiganDurable POA: either acknowledged before a notary or signed in front of two witnesses who are not agents [8]
OhioSigned; notarization is not strictly required, but a notarized signature is presumed genuine, which banks and title companies rely on [10]

Rules for health care powers of attorney, for real estate transactions and for POAs signed in another state can differ. A POA used to sell or mortgage real estate often has to be recorded with the county, which adds a recording fee. Check the current statute or ask a local lawyer before you sign.

The Uniform Power of Attorney Act

The Uniform Power of Attorney Act is a model law from the Uniform Law Commission meant to make POAs work more consistently from state to state [14]. States that adopt it, such as Michigan and Ohio, write it into their own codes [9][11], often with changes. Ohio's version shows the three features that matter most for cost:

  • A POA is durable unless it expressly says incapacity ends it, so you do not need special durability language [12].
  • A signature acknowledged before a notary is presumed genuine, which makes banks and other third parties more willing to accept the document [10].
  • "Hot powers," such as creating or changing a trust, making gifts, creating survivorship rights or changing beneficiary designations, exist only if the POA grants them expressly [13]. Deciding whether to grant them is where legal advice earns its fee.

Other states, including several in the table, have their own POA statutes, so your state's code is the better guide to what applies to you.

What drives the cost of a power of attorney

The out-of-pocket formalities are small. A California notary may charge up to $15 per signature [15], and witnesses are usually free. The real cost is legal time, which depends on:

  • Scope: a one-transaction limited POA takes less work than a general durable POA.
  • Hot powers: gifting, trust changes and beneficiary changes need careful drafting, especially in blended families or when Medicaid planning is involved.
  • Bundling: many lawyers quote a POA as part of an estate plan with a will and health care directive; a stand-alone quote can look high by comparison.
  • Capacity concerns: if the principal's capacity may be questioned, the lawyer may need extra meetings and documentation.
  • Multi-state property: owning real estate in more than one state can mean more than one document.

Example (hourly illustration): 1.5 hours for a meeting, drafting and supervised signing at Clio's national average of $349 an hour [16] = 1.5 × $349 = $523.50, plus a notary fee if the lawyer's office does not notarize for free. Many estate lawyers quote a flat fee instead; ask what it includes.

Online form or lawyer?

A form or statutory short form can work when the POA is limited to a specific task, your family situation is simple, you trust the agent completely and you follow your state's signing rules exactly. New York, for example, publishes a statutory short form with set execution steps [4].

Pay for a lawyer when you want to grant gifting or trust powers, you are planning for long-term care or Medicaid, the principal's capacity is in doubt, a family member is likely to object, or you own a business or property in several states.

Questions to ask

  • Is the POA durable, and does it take effect now or only on incapacity?
  • Which hot powers are included, and why?
  • Does the fee include notarization, witnesses and a supervised signing?
  • Is a health care POA or living will included in the same price?

Related reading: notary fees by state, will cost and estate planning lawyer cost.

faq.q: Does a power of attorney have to be notarized?
faq.a: It depends on the state. Texas, Florida, New York and Pennsylvania require notarization for a standard financial POA, while California and Michigan accept either a notary or two witnesses.

faq.q: How many witnesses does a power of attorney need?
faq.a: Florida and New York require two witnesses plus a notary. California and Michigan require two witnesses only if you do not use a notary, and Georgia requires a witness plus a second attestation.

faq.q: What is the difference between a durable and a regular power of attorney?
faq.a: A durable POA keeps working if you lose mental capacity, which is usually when it is needed most. A non-durable POA ends at incapacity.

faq.q: Can I make a power of attorney without a lawyer?
faq.a: Yes, many people use statutory or online forms, especially for limited POAs. The risk is in broad powers such as gifting and in getting the signing formalities wrong for your state.

faq.q: Is a POA from another state valid?
faq.a: Many states honor POAs that were valid where they were signed, but banks and title companies may still ask for their own forms or extra proof. If you move, have the document reviewed under your new state's law.
